observation:
**What's observable in this single rendered view**

**White target (left).** A space-filling (sphere/CPK) assembly of pale, off-white atoms occupying roughly the left third-to-half of the frame, spanning from about x≈325 to x≈690 px and y≈195 to y≈545 px. Its outline is irregular and lobed: an upper-left mass, a broad central bulge, and a lower pendant lobe descending toward the bottom-left. Sphere shading (bright specular highlights upper-left on each atom) is consistent across the group, indicating a single light direction.

**Cyan binder (right).** A larger, brighter cyan sphere-packed body occupying the right half, roughly x≈555 to x≈1035, y≈165 to y≈585. It reads as two stacked lobes — an upper band trending up-right toward the top-right corner, and a lower lobe dropping to the bottom edge near x≈700–790. Its left margin interdigitates with the white body rather than meeting it as a flat plane.

**Coral patch (center).** A narrow coral/salmon band sandwiched between the two, running diagonally from about (600, 150) at top down to (560, 400) at lower-left of the seam. It is not a contiguous slab in this projection: it appears as an upper cluster near the top, a mid-strip around y≈250–350, and one or two isolated coral spheres peeking through at roughly (555, 385) and (465, 405) — those lower ones are visible only through gaps in the white spheres.

**Occlusion assessment.** The coral patch is substantially occluded. In front, white spheres overlap its left edge and cyan spheres overlap its right edge; several coral atoms are clipped to thin crescents (e.g., the partial arcs near x≈640–685, y≈290–330). The rear face of the interface — anything on the far side of the contact seam along the view axis — is entirely hidden behind the two foreground bodies; there is no line of sight through the assembly at any point along the seam. The visible coral area is a thin sliver of what the legend implies is a two-sided contact region.

**Recommendation.** Yes — request the reverse contact-only view. From this camera you cannot determine (a) how far the coral patch extends behind the white body, (b) whether the rear seam is continuous or broken, or (c) the(c) the depth-wise extent of cyan/white interpenetration on the far side.

**What the reverse view should show**

- Hide or ghost the white and cyan bodies, render only the coral-flagged atoms, so the patch outline is unobstructed.
- Camera rotated 180° about the vertical axis from this frame, so the currently-hidden rear seam faces the viewer.
- Same light direction and sphere radii, so patch areas are visually comparable between the two frames.

**Supplementary frames worth adding**

- A top-down view (camera rotated 90° about the horizontal axis) to show how deep the seam runs along the view axis in the present image — this is the axis with zero information right now.
- A "split" frame with the two bodies translated apart along the seam normal, coral retained on both faces, to show which coral spheres belong to the white side and which to the cyan side. In the current render that assignment is unrecoverable, since the coral band reads as one strip regardless of which body each sphere sits on.

**Limits of what any of these frames establish**

These are geometry and visibility observations only — sphere overlap in projection, occluded regions, and camera coverage. Nothing here speaks to affinity, specificity, or efficacy, and the scene remains an illustrative translated pair rather than a design result. The "actions" implied by translating or rotating the bodies are camera and scene operations, not physical time evolution of the system.
